name: Trimax

lead: Trimax is the looksmaxxing term for combining bimaxillary (double jaw) surgery with a chin procedure. In practice that means moving the upper jaw (Le Fort I), the lower jaw (bilateral sagittal split osteotomy, BSSO) and the chin (genioplasty) in one plan.

The appearance payoff people seek is a more forward, balanced jaw and chin in profile, a better-defined jawline and a change in how the midface and lips sit. Orthognathic surgery in general is described as usually producing a noticeable change in the face, and planning software is used to preview results.

paras: Patients typically work with an orthodontist and an oral and maxillofacial surgeon: braces first to align the teeth, then surgery under general anaesthesia, then a period of liquid or soft diet and follow-up. Forum members describe travelling abroad for the operation, comparing surgeons, and sometimes adding facial implants, rhinoplasty or other procedures on top.

Reported risks of orthognathic surgery include bleeding, swelling that can last months, infection, and numbness from nerve injury, which usually resolves within about three months and is rarely permanent. Recovery involves weeks off work and dietary restriction. Forum users also discuss unexpected changes to the lips, nose and frontal appearance.

angle.text: Trimax changes the underlying bone position of the lower face, so the effect is structural rather than cosmetic cover-up. People pursue it to improve side-profile projection and overall facial harmony, with planning software used to preview the expected result.

lead: Trimax is a looksmaxxing term for triple jaw surgery: an operation in which the upper jaw, lower jaw and chin are all repositioned in one plan. It is double jaw (bimaxillary) surgery combined with genioplasty, and in forum culture it sits at the top of the 'hardmaxxing' ladder, the group of surgical and other invasive methods used by people who want to change the bony structure of the lower face. [1][2][3]

People pursue it to improve how the face looks from the side and the front. Moving the jaws and chin forward or rebalancing them can give a more projected chin, a more defined jawline and a different relationship between the lips, nose and lower face. Surgeons use photographs, X-rays and planning software to preview the expected outcome, and orthognathic surgery in general is described as usually producing a noticeable change in the face. [1][4]

Orthognathic surgery was developed to correct bite, airway and jaw-position problems, and it is also used for facial proportion and symmetry. The upper jaw is moved with a Le Fort I osteotomy, the lower jaw with a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy (BSSO, popularised by Hugo Obwegeser) and the chin with genioplasty, with the bones fixed by titanium plates and screws. [1][5]

On looksmax.org, trimax threads range from before-and-after journals and surgeon comparisons to questions about timing, age and what else may be needed alongside it, such as lip lifts, rhinoplasty or facial implants. Published clinical research uses terms such as bimaxillary surgery and genioplasty rather than 'trimax'. [2][6][7][8]

paras: Trimax combines three bone cuts. A Le Fort I osteotomy moves the upper jaw (maxilla); a BSSO splits each side of the lower jaw (mandible) so it can be advanced or set back; and genioplasty cuts and moves the chin bone, which is fixed with plates. Surgeons may also use implants for chin advancement. [1][5]

The term itself comes from looksmaxxing forums, where 'bimax' means the two-jaw operation and 'trimax' adds the chin. Threads discuss whether someone needs a full trimax or only a genioplasty, how much it can change a face, and whether younger patients should wait. [9][10][11]

Genioplasty (also called mentoplasty) can be done with implants or by sliding the chin bone, which is cut in a horseshoe shape, moved forward or back and secured with a titanium plate. It is described as a relatively simple operation that produces a noticeable change in profile; sliding osteotomies can give more dramatic results than implants. When a small chin comes with a significant overbite, orthognathic surgery is the route described for the bite, since cosmetic chin procedures do not change it. [5]

Jaw surgery itself is old: Simon Hullihen's 1849 case is credited as the first published example, osteotomies of the jaws developed in the 1940s, and Hugo Obwegeser popularised the BSSO. The field grew out of oral surgery and orthodontics, and was built around bite, breathing and jaw-function problems. [1]

The looksmaxxing use of the procedure is much newer. Wikipedia traces looksmaxxing to 2010s forums, including PSL-rating communities, and says it reached TikTok in the early 2020s, where maxillofacial surgery is listed among the 'hardmaxxing' options discussed alongside rhinoplasty. [3] 'Bimax' and 'trimax' are the community's shorthand for the combined operations, and they appear in thread titles on looksmax.org that ask how far such surgery can change a face. [10][12]

Mainstream coverage of looksmaxxing has included surgeons' warnings. Christine Stiles, a plastic surgeon at UT Southwestern, writes that jaw procedures such as bimaxillary osteotomy and Le Fort I advancement are permanent and usually reserved for congenital deformities or injuries, and that surgeries changing facial bone structure are major procedures. She advises consulting a board-certified surgeon who can explain realistic outcomes and preview jaw realignment with 3D imaging. [4]

Planning is a team effort, usually between an oral and maxillofacial surgeon and an orthodontist. Braces to align the teeth before surgery can take up to a year, and newer approaches include surgery-first protocols and clear aligners. Photographs and X-rays are standard, and software can predict post-surgery appearance to help planning and patient explanation. A psychological assessment is sometimes included. [1]

Surgery is done under general anaesthesia, and the jaw may be immobilised for 1-4 weeks. Older methods required wiring the jaw shut for several weeks, which is now rarely needed. [1] Maxillary movements can also change lip length and nose base position, which is why forum users ask about lip lifts or rhinoplasty. [13][14]

Members present trimax as a way to fix a recessed lower third of the face that cannot be changed by non-surgical means. Typical thread topics include asking for opinions on profile photos, comparing it to gonial or other facial implants, and estimating how far it could improve overall attractiveness. [2][12]

Patient accounts describe the process from orthodontics to surgery, including surgeries performed abroad. One 2-week post-operative account describes heavy swelling, pain control in the first day and eating through a syringe in the first week, and says the frontal view looked 'decently normal' with slightly more harmony. [6]
Some users also ask about secondary procedures, for example whether a rhinoplasty or otoplasty should be added, or whether a lip lift is needed after the upper jaw is moved. [13][15][14]

Members present trimax as the way to fix a recessed lower third of the face, which they say cannot be changed by non-surgical means. Typical thread topics include profile photo critiques, comparisons with gonial and other facial implants, and estimates of how far it could improve overall attractiveness. [2][10][12]

Surgeon selection is a recurring theme. One thread asks about a named surgeon for trimax with full facial implants, and a reply says the poster would not trust a surgeon who did not work with a particular implant designer, showing how community members rank providers. [7] Others describe surgery abroad, including at a public hospital in Croatia. [6]

Another thread advises patience for younger members before a bimax or trimax. [11] UT Southwestern's Stiles notes that teenage faces are naturally softer and rounder and that edited social media images can make a younger person look older, which she cites as a reason to see a surgeon before deciding. [4]

Orthognathic surgery has an extensive clinical literature, much of it on bite correction, airway and cleft-related problems; estimates in Wikipedia suggest nearly 5% of people in the UK or US have dentofacial deformities needing surgery beyond orthodontics. [1]

A 2014 study of 30 Class III patients (19 men, 11 women, mean age about 32) who had Le Fort I maxillary advancement and BSSO mandibular setback used standardised photographs and lateral X-rays before surgery and at 3 and 9 months. Seven anthropometric indices changed significantly at 3 months and eight at 9 months, with the upper lip lengthening and the lower face shortening. No patient in that study had genioplasty, and the authors note a weak chin after bimaxillary surgery may call for one. [8]

A review of the literature on genioplasty describes common minor effects such as swelling, bruising and temporary lower-lip numbness, and less common infection, implant displacement or nerve damage. Surgeon experience is described as reducing complications. [5]

General orthognathic literature describes initial healing of 2-6 weeks with bone union taking 2-4 further months, a liquid diet, possible weight loss and swelling that can last months. Return to work is typically 2-6 weeks. [1]

Documented risks include bleeding, infection (reported up to 7%), and numbness from injury to the inferior alveolar nerve, which usually recovers within about three months and is rarely permanent. Maxillary impaction carries higher risk than some other movements. [1]
Facial implants added to a trimax plan carry their own risks, and forum users discuss secondary procedures for the nose, ears or lips after the jaws move. [13][15][14]

No studies found. Research on orthognathic surgery in general exists, but the term trimax is not used in clinical literature. (Search hits for 'Trimax' in medical databases refer to unrelated products such as a hair serum or a dental instrument.)

Mainstream outlets including the BBC, The Guardian, NPR, Business Insider and Vice have covered looksmaxxing, according to Wikipedia, with coverage focusing on bonesmashing, mewing and influencers; surgeons are quoted warning about the risks of extreme methods. [3] Jaw surgery appears in this coverage as the established, surgeon-performed end of the spectrum, in contrast with do-it-yourself methods. [3][4]

timeline.event: Simon Hullihen publishes what is credited as the first jaw-surgery case. [1]
Jaw osteotomies (bone cuts) develop as a surgical field. [1]
A paper on combined nose and chin surgery is published, one of the early references on chin procedures. [5]
Hugo Obwegeser's bilateral sagittal split osteotomy becomes widely used and spreads through Germany and beyond. [1]
A study of 83 patients treated 1987-1991 links removing third molars during the same operation with a high rate of hardware infection. [1]
Raffaini reports orthognathic surgery under local anaesthesia with intravenous sedation, reducing the need for hospital stays. [1]
Looksmaxxing and PSL-rating communities on forums begin discussing jaw surgery as a route to changing facial structure. [3]
A study of 30 patients measures photographic and X-ray changes at 3 and 9 months after bimaxillary surgery. [8]
Looksmaxxing spreads to TikTok; mainstream outlets later cover jaw surgery and bonesmashing within it. [3]
